a: It is I who sinned and did great evil
p: Chronicles' Hebrew says 'I have surely done evil'. The same letters, read differently, give 'I the shepherd did evil'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Greek of Chronicles, as reported; KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: and I have surely done evil
readings.plain: It is I who sinned and did great evil

readings.w: Proposed correction in BHS, after 2 Samuel 24:17 in the Greek and in 4QSam-a as reported
readings.plain: It is I who sinned. I the shepherd did evil

why: The Masoretic Text of Chronicles reads vehara' hare'oti, "and I have surely done evil," and the Plain English Translation follows it. The editors of BHS suggest reading haro'eh, "the shepherd," for vehara', which needs only a small change in letters and matches the Greek of 2 Samuel 24:17 and, as reported, 4QSam-a. The shepherd fits "these sheep" in the next words. Since no manuscript of Chronicles has "the shepherd," the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and notes the possibility.

a: Ornan turned and saw the angel
p: The Hebrew says Ornan saw the angel. The Greek of Chronicles reads 'the king', as in Samuel.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.plain: Ornan turned and saw the angel

readings.w: Greek of Chronicles (Septuagint), as translated by Brenton; compare 2 Samuel 24:20
readings.en: and he saw the king; and he hid himself, and his four sons with him
readings.plain: Ornan turned and saw the king

why: In Hebrew, "the angel" (hammal'akh) and "the king" (hammelekh) differ by one letter. Samuel says Araunah saw the king coming (2 Samuel 24:20), and the Greek of Chronicles agrees; in the Greek it is also Ornan himself who hides, with his four sons, where the Hebrew has only the sons hiding. The Hebrew of Chronicles fits its own story, in which the angel has stood over the threshing floor since 21:15 and Ornan's sons hide from him, and the next verse says separately that Ornan saw David. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

p: The written Hebrew has 'his son'; the scribes' reading is 'my son', as the start of David's speech.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), scribes' reading (Qere); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv)
readings.plain: David said to Solomon his son

why: The consonants bnw read as "his son" make Solomon the object of the narrator's words: "David said to Solomon his son." The scribes read beni, "my son," making it David's first word to him, as in 22:11 and 28:9. Both make sense. The Plain English Translation follows the scribes' reading with most translations; the difference is only where David's speech begins.

p: The written Hebrew has Shelomoth; the scribes read Shelomith. The same two forms alternate in 26:25–28.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv); NIV, ESV, BSB
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), scribes' reading (Qere); KJV

why: Both forms are known names (Shelomith in 23:18; Shelomoth in 24:22, where the Izharite of 23:18 is meant), and in these lists they alternate for one man, so the spelling does not mark two people. The written text is followed here because it is the text itself, and most modern translations print it.

p: The son is called Zina in 23:10 and Zizah in 23:11. The Greek and one Hebrew manuscript read Ziza in both.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
Greek (Septuagint) and at least one Hebrew manuscript, as reported in BHS

why: In Hebrew script the letters nun and zayin look alike, so Zina and Ziza were easily confused. The person is surely the same as Zizah in 23:11. Most translations keep Zina here and add a footnote; the Plain English Translation does the same.

a: The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the first
p: The Hebrew reads only 'The sons: Jeriah'. Translations supply 'of Hebron' and 'the first' from 23:19.

readings.w: Text as restored from 23:19; KJV (in italics), NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: the sons of Hebron: Jeriah the first
readings.plain: The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the first

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)

why: The list in 23:19 reads "The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third and Jekameam the fourth," and this verse repeats it. The words "of Hebron" and "the first" were lost in copying (the Hebrew uvanay even looks like a damaged form). The Plain English Translation supplies them, as nearly all translations do; the shorter Masoretic wording is given here.

p: The written Hebrew has Shamur; the scribes read Shamir.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), scribes' reading (Qere); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv)

why: A difference of one vowel letter. All major translations follow the scribes' reading.

p: The Hebrew beno can be a name or the word 'his son'. It may mean 'his son' here.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) as usually printed; KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
Alternative reading recorded for the Leningrad Codex in the STEPBible data; many commentators

why: The same letters mean "his son," and the alternative reading recorded for the codex takes them so here and in 24:27. Read that way, Jaaziah is a son of Merari: "the sons of Jaaziah his son." Most translations print Beno as a name, and the Plain English Translation does too, but the note on this verse gives the other reading.

p: The written Hebrew has 'the prophets'; the scribes read 'who prophesied'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), scribes' reading (Qere); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv)

why: The written text calls the singers "the prophets"; the scribes read a verb, "those who prophesied." Either way the singers are linked with prophecy, as in 25:2–3 and 25:5. The Plain English Translation follows the scribes' reading, which matches the verbs in 25:2–3.

p: The Hebrew lists five sons and says 'six'. One Hebrew manuscript and some Greek manuscripts add Shimei, who appears in 25:17.

readings.w: One Hebrew manuscript and some Greek (Septuagint) manuscripts, as reported in BHS; NIV, ESV, BSB
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Codex Vaticanus (as translated by Brenton); KJV

why: The verse ends "six," but the Masoretic Text names only five, and 25:17 assigns the tenth lot to a Shimei who is not otherwise listed among the singers' sons. Some Greek manuscripts and at least one Hebrew manuscript name him here, though Codex Vaticanus, like the Hebrew, has only five names. The Plain English Translation adds him, as most modern translations do, on the strength of the count "six" and of 25:17; the KJV follows the Masoretic Text.

a: The first lot came out for Asaph, for Joseph.
p: Every other lot ends 'twelve'. The Greek has 'his sons and his brothers' with the first lot, and editors supply Joseph's twelve.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV
readings.en: the first lot came out for Asaph, for Joseph
readings.plain: The first lot came out for Asaph, for Joseph.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint) in part, and the reconstruction in BHS; NIV, BSB
readings.en: ... for Joseph: he and his brothers and his sons, twelve
readings.plain: The first lot came out for Asaph, for Joseph: he, his relatives and his sons, twelve.

why: Every other lot in 25:9–31 ends with "twelve," and the total of 288 in 25:7 needs Joseph's twelve. The phrase was probably lost when a scribe's eye skipped. The Greek, as translated by Brenton, arranges the verse differently: "the first lot of his sons and of his brethren came forth to Asaph the son of Joseph," and then gives Gedaliah as the second. It thus has "his sons and his brothers" with the first lot, but the clean "twelve" for Joseph is the editors' reconstruction. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew as it stands; readers who switch will see the fuller text, which is surely what the list meant.

p: The Greek has Hosah alone. It supports the view that Shuppim is a copying slip.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
Greek (Septuagint), as translated by Brenton ("to Osa westward")

why: Verse 15 ends with ha'asuppim, "the storehouse," and the name Shuppim in verse 16 may be that word written again by mistake (see the note). The Greek has no Shuppim, which fits that view. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew, as most translations do.

a: On the east were six Levites
t: Six Levites, or six a day?
p: The Hebrew says 'six Levites' on the east. The Greek gives 'six a day', like the other sides.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: on the east, the Levites, six
readings.plain: On the east were six Levites

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as translated by Brenton ("six watchmen in the day"); NRSV
readings.en: on the east, six a day
readings.plain: On the east were six a day

why: The north and south each have "four a day" (layyom), and the Greek gives the east "a day" as well. The Hebrew "the Levites" is odd here, since all the gatekeepers are Levites, and some scholars think it replaced "a day." The NRSV combines the two ("six Levites each day"). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

p: The Hebrew reads 'Ahijah'. The Greek reads 'their brothers', which differs by one letter.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint; so Brenton's translation, "the Levites their brethren"); NIV, BSB, NRSV
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV

why: A Levite named Ahijah is unknown elsewhere, and the verse reads as a heading for the treasurers named in 26:21–28. The Greek's "their brothers" (acheihem) differs from achiyyah by one final letter. Most modern translations follow the Greek, and so does the Plain English Translation.

p: Here the written Hebrew has Shelomoth and the scribes read Shelomith. The next verse has Shelomoth.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv); ESV
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), scribes' reading (Qere); KJV, NIV, BSB

why: Verse 26 has Shelomoth, and verse 28 Shelomith, for the same man. Here the written text, Shelomoth, is followed because it is the text itself and matches 26:26. The Plain English Translation gives each verse its own Hebrew form (see the variant on 26:28).

p: The Hebrew here has Shelomith. The Greek has Salomoth, the form of 26:25–26.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, BSB
Greek (Septuagint), as translated by Brenton ("Salomoth"); ESV

why: The man of 26:25–28 is one person, called Shelomoth in 26:25 (written text) and 26:26 and Shelomith here. The Greek has Salomoth in both places. The Plain English Translation gives this verse's Hebrew form, as it does for every name; readers who switch will see the single spelling of the Greek.

p: The Hebrew names Elihu. The Greek names Eliab, David's eldest brother.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
Greek (Septuagint), as translated by Brenton ("Eliab of the brethren of David"); NRSV

why: Eliab is David's eldest brother (2:13; 1 Samuel 16:6), and no brother named Elihu appears elsewhere, so many commentators prefer the Greek. But the Hebrew can stand: Jesse had a son not named in 2:13–15 (1 Samuel 16:10–11), and "brother" can mean a more distant relative. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

a: was never entered into the count
p: The Hebrew says the number did not go 'into the count' of the annals. The Greek has 'the book'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV
readings.plain: was never entered into the count

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as translated by Brenton ("not recorded in the book of the chronicles"); NIV, BSB
readings.plain: was never entered into the book

why: The Hebrew bemispar, "in the count," and besefer, "in the book," differ by one letter, and the word mispar, "number," stands just before. The Greek reads "book," which matches the way Kings cites "the book of the events of the days." The Hebrew makes sense as it stands: the number was never added to the official reckoning. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

p: The written Hebrew has Shitrai; the scribes read Shirtai.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), scribes' reading (Qere)

why: Two letters are swapped. English translations keep the written form.

a: For a second time they made David's son Solomon king
t: 'A second time' missing in some Greek
p: The Hebrew says Solomon was made king 'a second time'. Some Greek manuscripts lack the phrase.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); most Greek manuscripts (so Brenton); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: and they made king a second time
readings.plain: For a second time they made David's son Solomon king

readings.w: Some Greek (Septuagint) manuscripts, as reported in the commentaries; reportedly the Syriac
readings.plain: They made David's son Solomon king

why: "A second time" points back to 23:1, where David made Solomon king, or to the anointing at Gihon (1 Kings 1:38–40). Some scholars think a scribe added the word to harmonize the accounts; others that it fell out of the shorter manuscripts because it seemed to clash with them. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
